name: Yinbaw Karen
catalog_citation: Haudricourt, Andre-Georges. 1975. Le systeme des tons du karen commun. Bulletin de la Societe de Linguistique de Paris 70(1): 339-343.
catalog_quote: D'après les tableaux de Luce, et leur résumé par Jones, la catégorie V est confondue avec la VI en pwo, en blimaw, en Gèba, et même en palaychi [...] La distinction V/VI se trouve dans les langues pa-o, kayah, geko, yinbaw, paku et sgaw. La catégorie V ne représente pas dans les langues actuelles (sauf peut-être en yinbaw) un tonème indépendant, mais la série de mots qui ont un ton VI en pwo, et un ton II en sgaw.

new_statements.quote: D'après les tableaux de Luce, et leur résumé par Jones, la catégorie V est confondue avec la VI en pwo, en blimaw, en Gèba, et même en palaychi [...] La distinction V/VI se trouve dans les langues pa-o, kayah, geko, yinbaw, paku et sgaw. La catégorie V ne représente pas dans les langues actuelles (sauf peut-être en yinbaw) un tonème indépendant, mais la série de mots qui ont un ton VI en pwo, et un ton II en sgaw.
new_statements.translation: According to Luce's charts, and Jones's summary of them, category V is merged with VI in Pwo, Blimaw, Geba and even Palaychi [...] The V/VI distinction is found in the languages Pa-O, Kayah, Geko, Yinbaw, Paku and Sgaw. In the present-day languages category V does not (except perhaps in Yinbaw) constitute an independent toneme, but rather the series of words that have tone VI in Pwo and tone II in Sgaw.
new_statements.citation: Haudricourt, Andre-Georges. 1975. Le systeme des tons du karen commun. Bulletin de la Societe de Linguistique de Paris 70(1): 339-343.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the mirror copy archive.org scanned of BSLP 70.1); the passage is at extract lines 129-140, immediately before the running head '342 ANDRE-GEORGES HAUDRICOURT', i.e. p. 341 as A says. scanned text reads 'pa-0', '(sauf peut-être) en yinbaw)' and 'ton Il' exactly as A declared normalising. 'yinbaw' here is Luce's 1950s Yinbaw (Yinban) Karen list = kvu, no namesake. The remark is second-hand and comparative (Yinbaw keeps Luce's tone categories V/VI apart; V 'perhaps' an independent toneme only in Yinbaw); it implies lexical tone and says nothing about stress, so tone language, no stress statement / tone is the right reading.
new_statements.relation_note: Yinbaw enters Haudricourt's argument for a third proto-Karen open-syllable tone as one of the languages preserving the V/VI tonal split; no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yinbaw is treated as a lexical-tone language: in Luce's transcriptions it keeps proto-Karen tone categories V and VI apart (unlike Pwo/Blimaw/Geba), and category V may even surface as a separate toneme in Yinbaw; nothing is said about the number of Yinbaw tones or about stress/accent.
new_statements.exceptions: 'sauf peut-être en yinbaw' -- Yinbaw singled out as the one language where Luce's category V might be an independent toneme
new_statements.identity_note: 'yinbaw' here = G. H. Luce's 1950s Yinbaw (Yinban) Karen field list, the same doculect as the held Luce MS 6574-7-3 lexicon; Karenic, Kayah/S. Shan States; no namesake issue. Not listed by Glottolog under yinb1236 (Glottolog files Haudricourt's Karen papers under Sgaw/Pwo). | 'Yinbaw Karen, spoken by approximately 7,000 individuals in the Shan and Kayah states of Burma (to the southeast of the Lahta-speaking area)' = kvu; data are Manson's own Yinbaw fieldwork (Manson 2019 counts 4 Yinbaw dialects). File was placed in the mirror by the world-tree Stage-0 reader, not on verification

new_statements.quote: VII. Yinbaw. VII.1. General. The only extensive collection of data on Yinbaw Karen, spoken by approximately 7,000 individuals in the Shan and Kayah states of Burma (to the southeast of the Lahta-speaking area), is found in the as-of-yet unpublished fieldwork by Ken Manson [Manson Ms.], available to us in the form of Excel databases. A more or less complete Swadesh wordlist for Yinbaw has been extracted from that database. VII.2. Transcription. The transcription is essentially the same as for Pekon Kayan. [and under V.2 Pekon Kayan:] (c) a system of six tones is postulated, which can also be phonologically interpreted as four tones plus an additional parameter of breathiness.

new_statements.quote: Bennett, J. Fraser. 1992. Interim findings report: Central Karen investigation. ms / Classifies Kayan as “Central Karen”. Uses the names Padaung, Yeinbaw and Gekho. Notes that some Padaung dialects preserve final [ŋ], and that they preserve the breathy-modal phonation distinction. / [tone box] Padaung A B D: non-vd 4 1 2, voiced 4̤ 1̤ 3̤; Yeinbaw A B D: non-vd 5 1 5, voiced 3̤ 1̤ 5̤ / Bennett, J. Fraser. 1992. Phonetics and phonology of Karen languages. ms [...] Notes the retention of final [n, ŋ] in Padaung, but lost in Yeinbaw. Proto-voiced became voiceless with a register contrast (breathy phonation). Proto-stop final syllables remain distinct in both Yeinbaw and Padaung (no comment on Zayein or Gekhu).
new_statements.citation: Manson, Ken & Roslyn Manson. 2005. An Annotated Bibliography of Kayan. Chiang Mai: Payap University, Department of Linguistics, Graduate School. 9 pp. (SIL REAP copy; PDF metadata: 'Biblio of Kayan.doc', created 2005-03-22).
new_statements.locator: p. 2, entries 'Bennett, J. Fraser. 1992. Interim findings report' and 'Bennett, J. Fraser. 1992. Phonetics and phonology of Karen languages' (extracted textof the saved)
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold extracted text of the the Internet Archive SIL-REAP PDF) lines 31-47 = p. 2 carry exactly the two Bennett 1992 annotations and the Padaung/Yeinbaw A-B-D tone box A quotes; A only joined the two entries with ' / ', inserted '[tone box]' and elided the dialect-name list with '[..]'. p. 1 line 16 equates Kayan Kangan = 'Yinbaw', so Yeinbaw here is kvu. I searched all 307 lines for stress/accent/syllable/tone/register: 'stress' and 'accent' never occur; the other tone remarks concern Padaung/Pekon (Anon. dictionaries 5 tone symbols; Coolia 1980 3 tones; Manson Han Bo 6 tones incl. breathy), Gekho (4-5 tones) and the Jones 1975/1985 pointers to Yinbaw tone data from Luce's noteboo…
new_statements.relation_note: Tone only (second-hand tone box and register remark for Yeinbaw); no stress/accent remark anywhere in the 9 pages.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand (Manson's annotation of Bennett's unpublished 1992 reports): Yeinbaw/Yinbaw is treated as a lexical-tone language with a breathy (register) series from proto-voiced initials; Bennett's tone box gives Yeinbaw reflexes tone 5 (proto-tone A and D, plain initials), tone 1 (B), and breathy 3̤/1̤/5̤ after proto-voiced initials; final nasals lost in Yeinbaw. Nothing is said about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the annotation adds that proto stop-final syllables stay distinct in Yeinbaw
new_statements.identity_note: Listed in our bibliography only inside the composite 'Glottolog langdoc refs' record entry (never opened); now downloaded and read in full. The bibliography covers the whole Kayan cluster and names 'Kayan Kangan "Yinbaw"' as one of the four sub-tribes; the quoted annotations concern Yeinbaw = Yinbaw [kvu] specifically (Bennett's Yeinbaw data are the same field data Manson 2002/2003 used for 'Yeinbaw').
